domains.title: God of Fire and Volcanic Force
domains.subtitle: Creation, Destruction, and the Origin of Death
domains.lead: Kagutsuchi is the fire god whose birth burned his mother Izanami to death, introducing mortality into the mythic world. He is creation and destruction in one figure: the flame that forges and the flame that consumes. After his death at the hands of Izanagi, his scattered body became the volcanoes and hot springs of Japan.

cards.name: Birth of Fire
cards.desc: His birth from Izanami introduced both fire and death into the world.

cards.name: Slain by Izanagi
cards.desc: Izanagi avenged Izanami's death by cutting Kagutsuchi into pieces with the Totsuka-no-Tsurugi.

cards.name: Volcano God
cards.desc: His dismembered body became the volcanoes and geothermal springs of the land.

cards.name: Forge and Hearth
cards.desc: Fire for cooking, warmth, and metalwork descends from his power.

symbols.name: Volcano

symbols.name: Forge
symbols.meaning: Hearth and smithy — the domesticated half of his double nature.

mythology.lead: Kagutsuchi's mythology is brief and absolute: a birth that kills, a death that multiplies life, and a legacy of fire that Japan's volcanoes still preach. The Kojiki spends little more than a page on him — yet that page is the hinge of the whole cosmogony, for it is at his birth that the creator goddess dies and the world divides into the living and the dead.

myths.title: The Burning Birth
myths.text: After the islands were born, Izanami bore the last child of the creation — the fire kami Kagutsuchi — and his birth burned her. The Kojiki (I.8) tells it with terrible economy: the fire from the child's body scorched her, and from the agony of the wound the dying goddess brought forth still more kami — Kanayamabiko and Kanayamabime, the kami of metal, from her vomit; Haniyasubiko and Haniyasubime, the kami of clay and pottery, from her feces; and Midorikonomikami from her urine. Then, her body spent, Izanami died. She who had borne the islands and the thirty-odd kami of the land was destroyed by her final child: creation consuming its maker is the first law the new world teaches, and the fire god learned it in the only way a newborn can — by being it.

myths.title: The Blade of Grief
myths.text: Izanagi's grief turned to rage — 'Why must I lose my beloved for this one child?' — and drawing the Totsuka-no-Tsurugi, the ten-handled sword of the brine, he cut the fire kami down. What fell from the blade was life. From the blood on its point came Iwasaku and Nesaku, the 'stone-cutting' kami; from the blood on its hilt came Mizuhanome, the goddess of water who quenches fire; and from the severed body came the mountain kami whose peaks still steam along the Japanese chain (Kojiki I.9). The Nihon Shoki preserves variant versions of the same burning-birth and gives the child the parallel names Homusubi and Hi-no-Kagutsuchi. Kagutsuchi thus dies the only death in the cosmogony struck by a god's own hand — and the dismemberment, like the birth, manufactures gods: fire destroys, and destruction is revealed as one of generation's ordinary forms.

myths.title: The Child Who Created Death
myths.text: Because Izanami died, Izanagi followed her down to the land of Yomi; because he followed, he saw her body corrupted, guarded by the eight Thunder Kami; because he fled from the sight, Izanami cursed him, and the world split in two at the Even Pass of Yomi — Izanagi swearing to give life its thousand generations, Izanami to take a thousand a day. Then, purifying himself in the river of the plain, Izanagi washed from his left eye Amaterasu, from his right eye Tsukuyomi, from his nose Susano-o — the three sovereign children of the later pantheon (Kojiki I.10–11). None of it happens without the fire child's birth. Kagutsuchi is the pivot of the entire Japanese cosmogony: the instant at which the world of undying creators ends and the world of birth and death begins. One page of story carries every assumption the later shrines and epics must make — the sun included, for even Amaterasu exists because a fire once killed a mother.

myths.title: Homusubi, the Hearth
myths.text: The Kojiki gives Kagutsuchi no cult and no further adventures — his worship was the ordinary reverence of fire itself. Under the names Hi-no-Kagutsuchi and Homusubi, 'fire-producer,' he was honored at the hearth and the forge, where fire cooked, warmed, and smelted; fittingly, the metal and clay kami born from Izanami's dying body minister to the same fireplace and furnace. Folk tradition kept a careful double feeling toward him: fire was the gift no household could live without and the force that could erase the household in an hour, and in parts of Japan a prayer was still spoken before the first fire of the new year. This is the myth reduced to its element — no temples, no epics, only the daily negotiation between human beings and the one power in the house that must never be insulted. The volcanoes are his body; the kitchen fire is his ghost; both demand the same attention.

lore.syncretism: Comparisons come readily — Hephaistos and Vulcan as smith-fire, Agni as the god born who must be handled with care, Prometheus as the power that costs its bearer everything — but Kagutsuchi's closest relatives are his own siblings and victims: Izanami, whom his birth killed, and the metal and clay kami born from her dying body, who made his fire usable. Within Japan his identity overlapped with the folk hearth deity Kōjin and with the volcano kami of the great peaks; Buddhist Japan did not canonically adopt him, but shrine and temple practice alike made offerings to the hearth fire. His theology stays pointedly Japanese: not a forge-god of artisans nor a fire-thief of the gods, but the tragedy of fire itself — the child whose birth introduced death into the world and whose dismembered body is the landscape. Where other traditions send fire to humanity as a gift or a theft, Japan keeps it at home as a birth, and mourns it.
lore.culturalLegacy: Kagutsuchi survives wherever Japan's volcanoes are in the news — the country that monitors its peaks for eruption is, in the old language, watching over the scattered body of a god. His name circulates widely in modern fantasy and games as a volcanic or destructive kami, sometimes flattened into a monster, though the original story is more tragic than fearsome: a child destroyed for being born what he was. The geothermal energy industry has quietly theologized him in reverse, tapping the heat his body left in the mountains as power. And at every hearth and every forge the oldest layer of his cult persists without shrines — the simple, ancient caution that fire is a guest who must be fed, watched, and never insulted. His is the only major Japanese cult whose temple is a kitchen.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Kagutsuchi is the fire we cannot live without and cannot safely hold. His birth is the moment the mythic world loses its innocence: before him, Izanagi and Izanami created without dying; after him, creation has a price, and the price is death. His father kills him for it, and even that punishment backfires into generation — the blood and body make more gods than the birth destroyed.

He asks the question every technology asks. Fire is the first machine, and the myth encodes the entire human history of machines in a single page: power that cooks and warms, that forges tools and razes houses, that makes and unmakes on the same breath. Japan, sitting on his dismembered body, knows this geology literally. To honor Kagutsuchi is to keep a respectful distance from the flame — close enough to cook, far enough to survive the spark.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written 迦具土 — phonetic man'yōgana whose characters ('add', 'tool', 'soil') were chosen for sound, not sense. Later tradition sometimes writes the fire deity with the more transparent 火産霊 (Homusubi, 'fire-producing spirit').
lore.archaeology: Kagutsuchi left no temples, inscriptions, or cult images — the evidence for him is textual and geological. The textual witness is the eighth-century manuscript tradition of the Kojiki (712 CE) and the Nihon Shoki (720 CE), whose compilers fixed the story; the Shinpukuji-bon and the Urabe recension are its principal witnesses. The 'archaeology' of his body is the archipelago itself: the volcanic chain from Fuji to Aso to Sakurajima, with its crater shrines and steam vents, and the hot-spring country the Kojiki already reads as the fire kami's remains. And beneath the myth lie the oldest controlled fires on earth: the hearths of Jōmon pit-dwellings (from c. 14,000 BCE), where a culture learned to keep the exact double attitude the myth prescribes — fire fed daily, and feared daily. That hearths older than any shrine in Japan still govern his cult is the most honest monument he has.
